title: Freight broker vs. freight agent: choosing your business model
seoTitle: Freight Broker vs. Agent: Roles, Support & Commission
searchIntent: Should I open a brokerage or work as a freight agent?
excerpt: Compare brokerage ownership with freight agency work: responsibilities, support, commission arrangements and the questions to ask before signing.
takeaway: Compare the responsibilities and support behind the commission split. A higher percentage is only useful if the arrangement supports the work you need to do.

sections.title: Start with the responsibilities you want to own
paragraphs: Luis frames this decision around time, money and risk. Selling freight services is only one part of operating a brokerage. Someone must maintain the business infrastructure, manage credit, handle accounting, support operations and resolve problems when a shipment or payment goes wrong.

A freight agent arrangement can place some of that infrastructure with the brokerage. The actual division of work depends on the agreement. Before comparing income, identify who will approve customers, qualify carriers, provide systems, invoice shippers and handle collections.

sections.title: Understand what the commission split buys
paragraphs: A commission percentage does not describe the entire relationship. An experienced agent bringing an established book of business may need different support from someone learning to find and serve customers. Luis encourages evaluating what each side contributes.

If a hypothetical agreement divides $1,000 of eligible gross profit 70/30, the agent share is $700 and the brokerage share is $300. That arithmetic only helps once the contract defines eligible gross profit and any deductions. It is not a promised compensation arrangement.

sections.title: Ask how and when commissions are paid
paragraphs: Determine whether payment follows delivery, receipt of complete paperwork, shipper collection or another event. A signed proof of delivery and an invoice may start a process without triggering an immediate commission.

Ask who bears an unpaid customer balance and whether the brokerage must approve credit before a shipment moves. Also clarify how claims, billing disputes, quick-pay costs and other adjustments affect the amount owed. These questions belong before the first customer is tendered.

sections.title: Inspect the operational support
paragraphs: Luis’s point is that access to a brokerage’s authority is not the same as a complete support system. Ask who answers an urgent operations question and what happens when your usual contact is unavailable.

Review systems access, administrative assistance and any fees. A lower commission with useful support may be a different business proposition from a higher commission that leaves you doing nearly everything yourself. Compare the work and costs you would actually retain.

sections.title: Read the customer and exit provisions
paragraphs: Customer ownership, solicitation restrictions and termination provisions can materially affect the relationship. Do not assume that bringing a customer automatically means you can take that account elsewhere under any circumstances.

Have qualified counsel review the agreement for the applicable jurisdiction. This guide identifies business questions; it does not determine whether a restriction is enforceable or whether a particular worker classification is correct.

sections.title: Choose a model that matches your present capabilities
paragraphs: Map the work you can reliably perform today against the work your proposed partner will perform. Then compare the economics after systems costs, administrative time and realistic support needs.
The useful decision is not which title sounds more entrepreneurial. It is whether you have a clear, sustainable arrangement for selling, operating and getting paid for freight service.
